Is the pay rise worth the commute? Compare a job offer in cash and hours

Use a cash-flow bridge, annual pay-and-cost bars, a commuting-time comparison and a sensitivity matrix to examine a higher-paying job.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare take-home pay, work costs and commuting time

Interactive planning lab

Additional annual cash after the specified work costs$616
Additional commuting hours per year241.5
New monthly take-home pay to match current remaining cash$4,948.67

Original full-year job comparison in nominal CAD. Each monthly take-home amount is entered independently after payroll deductions and is received for all twelve months. Commuting days equal days per working week × the shared number of working weeks. Return-trip cash cost and return-trip time are entered per commuting day. Other work costs are constant monthly amounts incurred throughout the year. Take-home pay less these specified work costs is a partial cash comparison, not a complete household budget. Negative remaining cash is a deficit to fund separately. No tax, gross-to-net salary conversion, bonus, benefit, employer match, moving cost, start-date gap or pension valuation is calculated. Time is shown separately without assigning an hourly money value. Paid work hours, overtime, caregiving and job quality are outside the comparison. The entered amounts are assumptions, not observed salary or commuting statistics.

  2. The cash bridge subtracts the cost difference

The central idea

A higher take-home salary can leave only a small cash improvement after work costs. Show the time commitment separately before judging the offer.

01

Start with comparable take-home amounts

A job offer may advertise a higher salary while changing commuting, meals, parking, clothing, care arrangements and the time available at home. The useful starting comparison is the cash the household can actually receive, followed by the costs required to earn it.

The tool asks for monthly take-home pay in the current and proposed jobs. Enter independently estimated amounts after payroll deductions on the same basis. It does not convert gross salaries into net pay, estimate income tax or treat a discretionary bonus as certain. If the offer is quoted biweekly, use the actual annual payroll expectation before converting it to a comparable monthly amount.

The default moves from CAD 4,500 to CAD 5,000 of monthly take-home pay, a CAD 6,000 annual increase. That is a starting point rather than the final household improvement. Both amounts cover all twelve months; commuting occurs only during the selected working weeks. A partial first year or an unpaid gap between jobs needs its own dated cash plan.

02

The cash bridge subtracts the cost difference

The current job requires three commuting days per week for 46 weeks, at CAD 12 per return trip. Annual commuting cost is CAD 1,656. Other work costs are CAD 50 per month, adding CAD 600. The proposed job requires five commuting days per week at CAD 28 per return trip, producing CAD 6,440 of travel costs plus CAD 1,200 of other work costs.

Specified annual work costs therefore rise from CAD 2,256 to CAD 7,640, a CAD 5,384 increase. Subtracting that increase from the CAD 6,000 take-home improvement leaves CAD 616 per year, or about CAD 51.33 per month, before omitted household effects.

The waterfall subtracts the incremental costs. Subtracting all of the new commuting cost while ignoring the old cost would understate the gain; subtracting neither would overstate it. A cost that falls adds to the bridge. If the final step is negative, the offer leaves less cash under the entered assumptions despite any higher pay.

03

Include costs that actually change, and avoid charging them twice

Use the return-trip daily input for costs that vary with office attendance. Fuel and parking may fit this structure when the rate is reasonably stable. A monthly transit pass does not necessarily cost less because one office day is removed, so place a fixed pass cost in the monthly field instead of pretending it is entirely variable.

Other monthly costs can include a separately estimated change in work meals or clothing. Count only the relevant additional amount if an expense would also occur at home. Do not enter the same parking or travel bill in both fields. A new vehicle, relocation, child care or a substantial change in insurance needs more detail than this compact comparison provides.

The annual bars show take-home receipts and specified costs separately. Their difference is cash remaining before ordinary living expenses and saving, not a complete disposable-income statistic. The FCAC budgeting guide provides general context for tracking actual income and expenses. The salary amounts, cost schedule and calculations here are original hypothetical examples.

04

Read the time chart without inventing an hourly wage

The current return trip takes 45 minutes; the proposed trip takes 90 minutes. Across the default working weeks, annual commuting rises from 103.5 hours to 345 hours. That is an additional 241.5 hours travelling for the CAD 616 partial annual cash improvement.

The model leaves those hours visible rather than automatically assigning them a dollar value. A shorter trip may support caregiving, rest, study or another activity that the household values differently. Conversely, a role can offer development, stability or satisfaction that a cash-only comparison does not capture.

These are commuting hours, not total hours worked. Dividing annual take-home pay by this travel time would not produce a meaningful hourly wage. Differences in contracted hours, overtime, remote availability and unpaid responsibilities require separate inputs and judgment. The chart gives one time commitment a clear scale without pretending to evaluate the entire employment decision.

05

Use the break-even pay as a cash comparison, not a salary recommendation

The break-even metric asks what monthly take-home pay the new job would need to leave the same cash after the specified work costs. It equals (current annual remaining cash + proposed annual work costs) ÷ 12. With the defaults, the result is about CAD 4,948.67 per month.

That is a net-pay figure. It is not the gross salary to request from an employer, and converting it requires an independently appropriate payroll estimate. It also leaves out pension accrual, employer matching, insurance benefits, stock compensation and other non-cash terms. A higher break-even amount can result when new cash costs are substantial even though the advertised salary increase looks large.

The sensitivity matrix tests alternative office attendance and return-trip costs for the new job. Holding pay and other inputs fixed, three commuting days at CAD 28 per day would leave CAD 3,192 of additional annual cash in this example. That possibility is useful only if the arrangement is actually available and durable.

06

Build a decision record with money, time and unresolved terms

  1. Verify comparable annual take-home expectations and the first payment date.
  2. List work costs that change, separating per-day costs, fixed costs and one-time costs.
  3. Document the office schedule, return-trip travel time and whether either can change.
  4. Compare retirement and insurance benefits separately from current cash.
  5. Check how the transition affects reserves, care arrangements and existing commitments.

The illustration assumes a full year in each role, constant pay, a stable schedule and known costs. It does not model a probation period, future pay rises, job loss, changing travel prices or a late reimbursement. Use the result to locate the assumptions that matter, then test them against the actual offer and household budget before making a commitment.
